analysis.one_liner: Limits how much credit card debt companies can extend to full-time college students under 21.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in August 2007 and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped credit lines for full-time college students under 21 at a share of their own income (the greater of 20% of annual income or $500, and no more than 30% of income across all their cards). It also would have required written parental approval before raising limits on cards where a parent is on the hook for the debt, required issuers to verify a student's income and credit history before opening an account, and barred giving a second card to a student with no verifiable income who already holds one card from the same issuer. It never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time college students under 21, and the parents and guardians who co-sign or otherwise end up paying off their children's credit card debts. The caps and income-verification rules would have limited the debt students could take on before they had any income to repay it.

how_it_helps.text: Caps a student's credit line at the greater of 20% of annual gross income or $500, and caps total credit lines across all cards at 30% of income, unless a parent, guardian, or spouse assumes joint liability [S2] [S3].
Bars issuers from raising the limit on a card where a parent or guardian is jointly liable without that person's written approval and agreement to remain liable for the increase [S2] [S3].

Requires issuers to verify a student's income, income history, and credit history before opening an account, and prohibits opening a card for a student with no verifiable income who already holds a card from the same issuer or an affiliate [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose a marketing channel built on signing students with little or no income, and the families who currently absorb the resulting debts, who would instead face stricter access to credit for students.

drawbacks.text: Tightening access to credit could leave some students without a card for legitimate expenses like textbooks or emergencies, particularly students with no income who previously relied on credit cards as a stopgap [S3].

The rules would add compliance costs and verification requirements for card issuers, and the bill gave the Federal Reserve broad authority to grant exemptions, making the actual reach of the rules uncertain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection targets a real harm: issuers marketed cards to students with no income, and parents frequently ended up paying those debts. The income-based caps are a blunt tool that could block some legitimate borrowing, and the Fed's exemption authority softened the rules. On balance, the benefit to students and their families outweighs the cost to issuers, though the design is less flexible than income-based underwriting alone would be.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Herb Kohl introduced the bill on August 1, 2007, with Senators Sanders, McCaskill, Durbin, and Smith as original cosponsors [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction [S1] [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers are better off because the bill died: nothing limited the credit lines or marketing practices aimed at students during the 110th Congress.

for.name: Sen. Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sens. Sanders, McCaskill, Durbin, and Smith

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it stayed in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small list of supporters crossed party lines — three Democrats, one Independent, and one Republican — but with only six total sponsors it never generated a recorded floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have capped the credit lines issuers could extend to students without a co-signer and required income verification, cutting off a marketing channel that signs up students with little or no income. Its defeat left those practices unrestricted for the rest of the 110th Congress.

industries.industry: Parents and guardians of college students
industries.note: Families who co-sign or absorb their children's card debts would have gained a written-approval requirement before any credit limit increase and tighter limits on unsolicited student credit.
